about.title: La Habra Workplace Injury Claims
about.longDescription: La Habra's mix of warehouses, retail centers, and light industrial sites along corridors like Whittier Boulevard and Imperial Highway means workplace injuries happen in a variety of settings, from loading docks to delivery routes on La Habra Boulevard. Under California law, workers' compensation is typically the exclusive remedy against your employer, no matter who caused the accident. But that's not always the end of the story. When a subcontractor, equipment manufacturer, property owner, or another driver contributed to your injury, a separate third-party claim may be possible alongside your comp benefits. Because these two paths run on different rules and different clocks, we review both for you. Our team handles workplace injury claims directly — we'll evaluate what options might apply to your situation before time limits close in.

whyChoose.title: Why La Habra Workers Choose Us

items.title: Understanding Your Two Possible Paths
items.desc: Workers' comp is usually the exclusive remedy against your employer, but a negligent third party can open a separate claim. We help sort out which applies to your case.

items.title: Deadlines That Don't Wait
items.desc: You generally have 30 days to report a workplace injury to your employer, and a third-party claim carries its own 2-year deadline. Missing either can limit your options.

items.title: No Cost, No Retaliation Risk
items.desc: California law prohibits employer retaliation for reporting an injury, and our consultation costs nothing upfront.

items.question: I was hurt working near Imperial Highway in La Habra — can I still file a claim?
items.answer: Location doesn't change the basic rules: you'd typically report the injury to your employer within 30 days and rely on workers' comp for medical care and lost wages. If a third party, like a delivery contractor or equipment supplier, contributed to the incident, a separate claim tied to that 2-year deadline may also be worth exploring.

items.question: Can I sue my employer directly for a workplace injury?
items.answer: In most cases, no — workers' compensation is the exclusive remedy against your employer regardless of fault. However, if someone outside your employer, such as a subcontractor or manufacturer, played a role in the accident, a separate third-party claim may still be available.

items.question: What if my employer retaliates after I report an injury?
items.answer: Retaliation for reporting a workplace injury is illegal under California law. If you believe you've faced retaliation, we can help you understand your options alongside your existing claim.

items.question: Is there a cost to contact you about my workplace injury?
items.answer: No. Our initial consultation is free, and we typically work on contingency, meaning there's no fee unless there's a recovery.
